Men are to be loved, sins to be hated, [unclear]. Let them hate sins, not men. Let the proud be corrected; let the weak be borne with; and those whom it is necessary to chastise more severely are to be punished not with the spirit of one raging, but of one healing.

Everyone is to be pitied; the sinner is to be angered at. 23 q. 4. These two names, when we say “man” and “sinner,” move us; in vain do they say: because he is a sinner, correct him; because he is a man, pity him. Nor will you wholly free the man unless you have persecuted the sinner. These things are Augustine’s, on the Psalter.

XXI

The manner and form of celebrating the provincial chapter of the fathers of the Order of Saint Benedict of the province of Mainz.

Since, in celebrating provincial chapters, many occupations are accustomed to confront the lord presidents, lest, when those well-worn and experienced have departed or are absent, those less experienced and not accustomed to celebrating chapters of this sort should happen to be distracted by those very many occupations, I have taken care to commit the present form in writing for the knowledge of those who follow. I saw and heard it in those very chapters at which I was often present when they were being celebrated. Although in it we do not have all the things that are to be done in chapters, nevertheless many things, and the more necessary ones, will be found. For I judge that this is useful both for those present, in the exercise of discipline, and for those to come, by the example and regard of their predecessors.

That the presiding officers, visitors, and treasurers should arrive before the day of the chapter.

Therefore the presidents, past and future, together with the visitors or treasurers, should arrive some days before the appointed day for celebrating the chapter, being meanwhile also supported at the expense of the chapter, in order to discuss and mutually advise one another on the things that arise to be done, as was ordained in the fifteenth chapter, celebrated for the second time at Seligenstadt in the year of the Lord 1454.

On the Saturday preceding the day of the chapter, let one citation be made of those absent and of those who have not yet made satisfaction concerning the imposition of the contribution. The promoter of the order, by mandate of the lord presidents, shall have this citation affixed by the notary of the chapter to the doors of the monastery under vespers or compline. And he shall have it similarly done in two other churches, if need be. The citation may be made under this form.

By mandate of the reverend [unclear] of the black monks of the Order of Saint Benedict of the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg, all and each of the abbots, provosts, and priors of the order of the province are here cited

of the aforesaid province and diocese, being bound to attend the chapter to be held on the coming Sunday Jubilate in the monastery of Saint N.; that they appear in person, or through their lawful proctors, on such a day at the sixth hour in the morning in the said monastery, before the aforesaid lord presidents, to show that they have obeyed the commands of the visitors and have truly and effectively satisfied the contribution imposed, and to hear other matters concerning the aforesaid things declared and pronounced. But if they have not appeared within the appointed time, then by those lord presidents proceedings will be taken against them as contumacious, as the order of equity shall dictate, according to the tenor of the privileges of the oft-mentioned order, the absence of those cited notwithstanding. In witness of all these things the seals of the two presidents are impressed. Given in the year etc., on such a day etc.

The notary should subscribe himself to this citation according to custom, and should make execution under vespers or compline.

The one who is to deliver the sermon on the morrow, on Saturday, should present it in writing to the lord presidents for examination and correction, if need be, lest scandal arise.

The former presidents should, before the day of chapter, render to the future presidents a full account of receipts and expenses, which they may read in the prior writings if there is need. And therefore on Wednesday both are ordered to arrive at the chapter, as was lately established in chapter 17.

On Sunday let the sign for terce be made earlier, in the year of the Lord 14[unclear]9, according to the ordinance of the presidents; and the abbot appointed to sing the mass should vest himself with the ministers, and at the introit should enter the choir, as is customary. And before the presbytery with the ministers he should read the Confiteor; and the mass of the Holy Spirit should be sung solemnly, at which all the priors are to be present.

When the mass is finished, let a lectern be prepared at the head of the choir. And let a conference be held for the priors and any others wishing to be present, concerning religion, discipline and humility, virtues and perseverance. The preacher, however, before he begins the sermon, [unclear]

[unclear]

should ask a blessing from one of the presidents, who is the principal one, if he is present. When the sermon is finished, let them enter the chapter place and let each sit: first the abbots, then the provosts and priors, and the proctors of the absent, according to the placing of the promoter. XXII Then the promoter, standing while all listen, should say:

In the name of God, amen. By the mandate of the venerable lord presidents, I warn and require all and singular here present, to whom it does not pertain to be present at this our sacred provincial chapter, under penalty of excommunication and suspension, to go out from this chapter place and withdraw. The notary shall remain with the witnesses; yet even they too may be ordered to go out while secret matters are being treated. These, afterward, if they are to be written down in recess, shall also be recited to the notary. Then, according to the usual custom, let them read from the martyrology, and let the Precious be added by the prior of the convent, after first asking a blessing from the president, saying: Lord, bid a blessing. And the president who gives the word should answer: May the almighty and merciful Lord direct us in the way of his commandments. And all should answer: Amen. And for the regular reading let him read from the second chapter of the Rule, concerning what sort the abbot ought to be. Chapter 2 of the Rule.

The abbot who is worthy to preside over a monastery should always remember what he is called, and should fulfill the name of superior by his deeds; he is believed to act in Christ's place in the monastery, since he is called by his own title, as the Apostle says: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, in which we cry, Abba, Father. Therefore the abbot ought neither to teach, nor establish, nor command anything outside the commandment of the Lord, which God forbid; but his command or teaching should be sprinkled like the leaven of divine justice in the minds of the disciples. This section is [unclear] most often customarily read as an opening. The abbot [unclear], because an examination must be made in the dread judgment of God concerning both matters, his teaching and the obedience of the disciples. And let the abbot know that the fault of the shepherd is incumbent, whatever in

for which [unclear] he will be less able to find advantage. Likewise he will be free if every diligence of the shepherd has been applied to a restless or disobedient flock, and every care has been shown for the diseased actions of them. Let their shepherd, absolved in the judgment of God, say with the prophet to the Lord: “I have not hidden your justice in my heart. I have declared your truth and your salvation”; but they, despising it, rejected me. And then at last, for the sheep disobedient to his care, the prevailing punishment is death itself.

He ought to preside over his disciples with a twofold teaching: that is, he should show all good and holy things by deeds more than by word, so that to capable disciples he may set forth the Lord’s commandments in words, but to those hard of heart and simpler, he may demonstrate the divine precepts by his own deeds. But let him show by his own actions that the things he has taught his disciples to be contrary are not to be done, lest, preaching to others, he himself be found reprobate, lest sin should ever say to him: “Why do you recount my justices and take up my covenant in your mouth? But you have hated discipline and have cast my words behind you.” And: “You who saw the speck in your brother’s eye did not see the beam in your own.”

Let no distinction of persons be made by him in the monasteries. Let one not be loved more than another, unless he has found him better in good deeds or obedience. Let the freeborn not be preferred to one converted from servitude, unless some other reasonable cause exists. But if, with justice dictating, it shall seem good to the abbot, let him do this from whatever rank. Otherwise let them keep their proper places, because whether slave or free, we are all one in Christ, and under one Lord we bear the equal service of soldiership; for there is no acceptance of persons with God. We are distinguished before him in this part only: if we are found better than others in good works and humble. Therefore let equal charity be shown by him to all; let one discipline be applied by him to all according to their merits.

XXIII

For in his teaching the abbot ought always to observe that apostolic sentence, in which it says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke”; that is, mingling seasons with seasons, caresses with terrors. Let him show the sternness of a master and the pious affection of a father: that is, he ought to reprove the undisciplined and restless more harshly; the obedient, gentle, and patient he should entreat, that they may advance toward the better; but the negligent and contemptuous we admonish him to rebuke and correct. And let him not dissemble the sins of offenders, but as soon as they have begun to arise, let him cut them out by the roots before they prevail, mindful of the danger of Eli the priest of Shiloh. And indeed, the more honorable and intelligent souls he should correct with words at the first or second admonition; but the wicked, hard, proud, or disobedient he should restrain at the very beginning of sin by blows or bodily chastisement, knowing that it is written: “The fool is not corrected by words.” And again: “Strike your son with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from death.”

The abbot ought always to remember what he is, and to remember what he is called, and to know that from him to whom more is entrusted, more is required. And let him know how difficult and arduous a task he has undertaken: to govern souls and to serve the characters of many. And one he must guide with caresses, another with rebukes, another with persuasions; and according to each one’s quality or understanding, let him so conform and adapt himself to all that he may not only suffer no losses in the flock entrusted to him, but may rejoice in the increase of a good flock.

Before all things, lest by dissembling or making little of the salvation of the souls entrusted to him he have greater concern for transitory, earthly, and perishable things, let him always consider that he has undertaken souls to be governed, concerning whom he will have to render account. And lest perhaps he should make excuse about lesser substance, let him remember what is written: “First seek the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things will be added to you.” And again: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear God.” And let him know that he who undertakes souls to be governed must prepare himself to render account; and however great a number of brothers he knows he has under his care

...of souls. Let him know for certain that on the day of judgment he will render to God an account for the souls of all those men, his own soul also without doubt being added. And thus, always fearing the examination to come, a pastor, when he takes care concerning the accounts of others, is made solicitous concerning his own.

When these things have been finished, or as much has been read as shall please those presiding, immediately from the book of the monastery let the names of the dead be recited, if any occur. Then, from the slips brought by the priors, let the names of the brethren of the order who have died since the last chapter celebrated be recited by the same reader of the martyrology. When these have been finished, let the presider add: “May the souls of the brothers, familiars, and benefactors of our order rest in peace.” And when the others have said “Amen,” let them read, as is customary, the psalm De profundis to the end, concluding with Requiem eternam. And when each has said silently the Pater noster, let the official add: “And lead us not,” etc., as is contained in the proceedings of the daily chapter. When these things have been completed, let one of those presiding enjoin upon the abbot of the house that after vespers the brothers perform vigils for those dead in choir. And let him appoint from among the priors one who on the morrow shall solemnly sing the high mass for the same dead. After this the promoter of the order shall read chapter In singulis from the Decretals, thus: Innocent III in the general council.

In each kingdom or province

In each kingdom or province, every three years, with the right of the diocesan bishops preserved, let there be held a common chapter of abbots and priors who do not have their own abbots and who have not been accustomed to celebrate such a chapter; to it let all come who do not have a canonical impediment, at one of the monasteries suitable for this purpose, with this moderation applied: that none of them bring more than six mounts and seven persons. But in the beginnings of this innovation let them call in two neighboring abbots of the Cistercian order, to furnish them suitable counsel and aid, since from long custom they are more fully informed in celebrating chapters of this kind; and these, without contradiction, shall associate with themselves two from among them whom they judge expedient. Let these four preside over the whole chapter in such a way that from this none of them assume to himself the authority of prelacy; and, when it is expedient, one already provided may be changed by deliberation. Let a chapter of this kind be celebrated for certain continuous days, according to the custom of the Cistercian order; in it let there be diligent discussion concerning the reformation of the order and regular observance. And what has been enacted, with those four approving, shall be inviolably observed, all excuse, contradiction, and appeal being removed; nevertheless provision having been made where the chapter ought to be celebrated at the next term. And those who have assembled shall lead a common life and shall all together meet the common expenses proportionally, so that, if not all can be together in the same house, at least several may dwell together in different houses.

Let them also ordain in the same chapter religious and circumspect persons who, according to the form prescribed to them, shall in our stead take care to visit each abbey of the same kingdom or province, not only of monks but also of nuns, correcting and reforming what they shall see to need the office of correction and reformation; so that if they recognize that the ruler of a place must be removed entirely from administration, they shall report him to his own superior, that he may see to removing him. And if he does not do so, let the visitors refer this to the examination of the apostolic see. The things that follow in this chapter are not customarily read consequently. The following chapter shall continue: Honorius III to the abbots and monks established in Lombardy and the March of Treviso.

Those things which for the honorableness of religion and [unclear]. Further, when the visitors appointed according to the statute of the general council have proceeded from the general chapter of abbots to carry out the office of visitation, let them diligently inquire concerning the state of the monks and regular observances; let them correct and reform, both in spiritual matters and in temporal matters, what they shall see ought to be corrected...

so nevertheless that he have delinquent monks corrected by the abbot of the place, and that salutary penance be imposed on them according to the Rule of blessed Benedict and the apostolic statutes, not according to the standard of the corrupt custom which, as if for law, has taken root in certain churches. The visitors themselves also, if they find any monks contumacious and rebellious, shall, in our stead, strike them with regular censure according to the measure of their fault, without respect of persons, not sparing rebels, because of their obstinacy, through the power of friends, but rather casting out the diseased sheep lest it infect the sound sheep. But if abbots are found negligent in correcting, according to the mandate of the visitors and the regular statutes, either themselves or their monks, let them be denounced and reproved, and so punished publicly in the general chapter that their punishment may be an example to others. But if an abbot who is not exempt is found by the visitors excessively negligent and lax, they shall without delay report this to the diocesan of the place, and by him let a faithful and prudent coadjutor be given to him until the general chapter. But if he is found to be a dissipator of goods, or otherwise deserving to be removed, after this has been reported to him by the visitors he shall be removed by the diocesan, without the din of legal proceedings, from the government of the abbey; and meanwhile let a suitable administrator be provided for the monastery, who shall take care of its temporal affairs until provision has been made for the monastery itself concerning an abbot. But if perhaps the bishop is unwilling to fulfill these things or neglects them, the visitors or those presiding over the general chapter shall not delay to make known the bishop’s default to the apostolic see. We command that these same things be done concerning exempt abbots by the visitors or those presiding over the general chapter, the deposition of those abbots being reserved to the apostolic see, so that, when an abbot who seems fit to be removed has meanwhile been suspended from administration by the visitors or by those presiding in the chapter, a suitable administrator shall be assigned to the monastery. The presiding officers, however, shall report to us, through faithful and prudent messengers, their excesses and the other matters which shall have seemed fit to be made known to the chapter; and to these messengers expenses shall be sufficiently supplied from the common contribution of the abbots, according to each one’s means.

The following visitors, however, shall diligently inquire into the traces left by the earlier visitors, and shall report their negligence and excesses to the next general chapter, so that they may publicly bear the penalty due according to their fault. We command the same to be observed also concerning the abbots presiding over the general chapter. And after a few words: We command that all these things also be observed in monasteries which do not have their own abbots but priors, and also in monasteries of nuns, so far as concerns the articles suitable for abbesses and nuns.

Then, if those presiding have ordered it, also the following.

From the constitution of Pope Benedict XII, on provincial chapters, chapter 2.

We also decree and ordain that in the order or religion of the aforesaid black monks, in each of the provinces deputed by us below, there shall be held every three years, in a place to be deputed for this purpose, saving the right of the diocesan bishops, a common or provincial chapter of abbots and of priors who do not have their own abbots, and of other priors of cathedral churches of that same order or religion, or of others who are greater in those churches after their prelates, by whatever name they are called, and of the other prelates who, as was said above, do not have their own abbots, exempt and non-exempt, of the same order or religion. To this chapter, unless a just impediment prevents them, all the aforesaid abbots, priors, and other prelates shall assemble, and in regard to the reformation of such order or religion and to regular observance they shall strive to fulfill the things set forth in the same constitution.

But those who shall not be able to come in person to that chapter, in order to allege the cause of a just impediment, shall send a monk of their own from the same church or monastery, if this can conveniently be done; otherwise another suitable man, with a sufficient mandate, a sufficient cause of excuse, and also power [unclear].

expressing that the cause of this kind is true, and swearing to it on their souls, they are bound to send it to the said chapter: with the judgment of the presidents of provincial chapters of this kind reserved, whose authority is to continue from one provincial chapter to another, so that at their discretion they may be able to decide whether the cause of excuse, or the excuses, when they have been variously alleged, are sufficient or insufficient; and that it is not lawful for anyone frivolously to appeal from their decree on this matter, or to protest in any other way whatever.

But those who do not come, when a lawful impediment has ceased, or who do not send to it, as has been stated above, an excuser and procurator, their fellow monk or another suitable person, with a sufficient mandate, are bound to pay, within a term to be fixed by the same presidents, double what they would have spent in coming to the said chapter, remaining in it, and returning from it, to be estimated according to the judgment of the same presidents or of the greater part of them, and to be converted to the use of that provincial chapter; and the presidents themselves may coerce them, by ecclesiastical censure and by the authority [apostolic?] applied, to pay this double amount, and may publish, or cause to be published, in the places of the same order or religion, the proceedings to be carried out against them in this matter and the sentences to be pronounced. And no grace may be granted or remission allowed concerning this double payment, either in whole or in part. And nevertheless proceedings are to be taken against the aforesaid absentees, especially if they maliciously withdraw themselves, or in order to avoid correction, or so that the condition of their church or monastery may not be known, or otherwise as shall seem good to the said presidents or to the greater part of them, their absence notwithstanding.

Concerning the presidents also and the visitors to be appointed in the same chapters, and all other things to be carried out in them, let those things be observed which are contained in the constitutions of the said general council and of Honorius, pope of happy memory, our predecessor; the statutes, ordinances, and additions of ours written above and below being nevertheless observed, in the manner in which they are modified and restricted in the same.

And because the instruction and salutary observance of the prelates and monks of that order or religion is involved, we decree that the priors of cathedral churches of the same order or religion, or those who are greater in those churches after their bishops, and after those bishops have regular care of the monks, by whatever name they are called, are to assemble in those provincial chapters under the modes and penalties designated above; and also that the same priors or greater persons and chapters, and all the monks of those churches or monasteries, even if in those churches or monasteries, or outside them, wherever they have priories, offices, or administrations, or have taken up residence, both exempt and non-exempt, even if those non-exempt persons are subject to certain exempt bishops, are included and also comprehended under the constraints and ordinances of the said provincial chapters; and that the aforesaid priors or greater persons, by apostolic authority, through ecclesiastical censure and other appropriate remedies, with the obstacle of appeal removed, are to compel them to observe these ordinances under the penalties which the said presidents shall think fit to impose on them, and also to compel any monks whatsoever of the aforesaid churches, holding monastic benefices pertaining to those same churches, to contribute to the moderate and reasonable expenses which the said priors or greater persons have incurred in coming to those chapters, staying in them, and returning from them.

And that any ordinaries of places, exempt and non-exempt, should place no impediment upon the aforesaid persons or any single one of them, nor permit one to be placed, but, when lawfully required at the proper times, should cause all and singular these things to be committed to execution and inviolably observed.

Indeed, intending to provide against the possibility that an impediment occurring to the meeting of any provincial chapter might be able to harm [unclear].

… and we will that, if it should happen that monastic cathedral churches, with priors or others existing in them as superiors after their bishops, as is stated above, or monasteries or places of the same order or religious estate, should be vacant or lack their pastors, who would be bound to assemble in the aforesaid provincial chapter at the time, namely, when the celebration of that provincial chapter is imminent, the chapters of the churches and the convents of the monasteries and of the other aforesaid conventual places shall be bound to send to the said chapter a sufficient person from the body of those same churches, monasteries, and places, if this can conveniently be done, or else a suitable person from elsewhere, for doing and fulfilling all things that the abbots, priors, or superiors in those cathedral churches, or the aforesaid others presiding in those same conventual places, could do if they had come to that chapter and were personally present in it.

But what is set forth concerning the provincial chapter to be celebrated every three years, in order to remove every scruple of hesitation, we wish to be referred to a sound understanding: namely, that when the provincial chapter has been celebrated in one year, in the next following year it may be omitted, and it shall take place in any case in the third year following.

Indeed, since it would be superfluous to issue sanctions if their execution were neglected and there were no one to protect them, we ordain and will that the said [common place?] or place of the religious estate suitable for this, if it exists in the same province, ought to be used for the celebration; otherwise it is to be celebrated in another fitting and secure place. Concerning this, and concerning the day for celebrating the first chapter of this kind, and concerning the other things to be done opportunely about the same matter, those who shall have been deputed for this by the Apostolic See shall provide on the first occasion.

And so that, concerning the same chapter and through it from then onward and perpetually, a reasonable ordinance may be had, we decree that in the said chapter first to be celebrated, and always thereafter successively, those presiding over the individual chapters to be celebrated, or the greater part of them, shall provide and take care to ordain by whom in the following chapter the sermon is to be delivered and Mass celebrated; and they shall choose the place for celebrating the next occasion of the aforesaid chapter, and who ought to preside in it. And thus let it be done thenceforth in successive provincial chapters.

They shall also provide which abbots, and how many, and how often, ought to visit the monastic cathedral churches, monasteries, and other places of the same order or religious estate up to the next provincial chapter itself. If it seems necessary to the lords presiding, the following chapter from the same constitutions of Benedict XII, On subventions and collections, may also be read. Likewise from the Benedictina, chapter 5.

Since in the often-mentioned constitution of the general council, among other things, it is expressed that those who have assembled in the triennial chapter are to lead a common life and proportionally meet the common expenses to be incurred, we, considering that besides expenses of this kind other expenses are necessarily required not only for the provincial but also for the aforesaid annual chapters, decree and ordain that in the same chapters, notwithstanding the contradiction or absence of anyone, for liberties, necessities, utilities, common expenses, and other customary matters, since a burden divided into parts is borne more lightly, collections, subventions, or contributions are to be made, imposed, and proclaimed by apostolic authority, according to the judgment of the presidents or definitors with regard to a provincial chapter of this kind, or of the abbot or other person presiding over the annual chapter itself and of the definitors with regard to the aforesaid annual chapter.

And so that in the preservation of collections, subventions, or contributions of this kind a precaution of security may faithfully be had, we will and ordain that the collections which shall be made in a provincial chapter, through three upright and faithful abbots or other prelates of that order or religious estate of that province in which the same chapter shall have been celebrated, in some secure monastery

or in another suitable place. But those which shall be made in the individual churches, monasteries, or other places of the same order or religious body shall be made by three upright and faithful monks of each church, monastery, or place in which, as stated above, they shall be made; of these, one shall be appointed by the abbot or other prelate of that place, another by the prior or priors and administrators or officers, and the third by the chapter of the church or the convent of the monastery or place of this kind. They shall be diligently kept in one chest locked with three locks, and shall be applied only to the use of those for whom they were made, and to no other uses. For faithfully observing and fulfilling these things, the said three abbots shall take a bodily oath in the presence of the presidents, and the aforesaid monks in the presence of the abbot and chapter, and also of the convent of the church or monastery, or of the prelate of the other principal place where the said annual chapter shall have been held. Nor may another contribution be made so long as anything sufficient from the first contribution happens to remain.

And let the aforesaid presidents, and each of them, who [unclear] to provincial chapters of this kind, as also abbots and superiors or the other already-named persons, have the power, by the authority applied above, of demanding, collecting, and levying collections, subsidies, and contributions of this kind from all and singular abbots subject to them, if they have or shall have any, and from priors, prelates, administrators, officers, and beneficiaries of whatever kind who shall be subject to that annual chapter, or to the church or monastery or other principal place; and of compelling all and singular the aforesaid persons, by the same authority and without appeal, through ecclesiastical censure and the other remedies of law and of the order or religious body itself, to pay in full the aforesaid collections, subsidies, and contributions, as shall have been ordained in such provincial and annual chapters, with terms assigned concerning this; and freely to publish and execute the aforesaid things, and processes and sentences in cathedral churches, monasteries, and other places of the same order or religious body, whenever and as often as it shall seem expedient to them; and also to absolve from the said sentences, provided that fitting satisfaction has first been made; and to relax and remove all processes and sentences of suspension and interdict; and to dispense with them concerning irregularity, if, being so bound, they shall have incurred any by profaning the divine offices, or otherwise involving themselves in them, yet not in contempt of the keys.

When these things have been read by the promoter of the order, other things also from the constitutions of earlier chapters may be read at the pleasure of the lord presidents. When all these things have been completed, one of the presidents, beginning the provincial chapter, shall say: “Bless ye.” Let the response be: “The Lord.” And again let him add: “Let us now speak, venerable fathers; from the sacred canons concerning the order [unclear] and from the constitutions of the supreme pontiffs you have heard the authority of this sacred provincial chapter, to celebrate which God has gathered us together into one; supported by that authority, we begin this provincial chapter itself in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.” Then let him add:

“We protest, therefore, first, that we wish this place and the other places of this monastery necessary for us for celebrating this chapter of ours to be assigned to us, and we assign them as a capitular place. And we wish this protestation to be held as repeated as often as, being assembled capitularly in the same places or in any one of them, we shall ordain, establish, or discuss anything.” Then the same president shall receive from the notary a manual promise that the acts of the chapter will be kept secret and not revealed publicly. And let the promoter say:

“We protest further that if anyone excommunicated, suspended, or interdicted is here, we do not intend to celebrate this chapter in his presence; therefore, if anyone knows himself to be such, let him leave this capitular place, and let him not presume to be present unless absolved.” And, turning to the notary, the same promoter shall add:

And you, lord scribe, I require with due urgency that you note this act and the following ones diligently, and enter them among the acts of the chapter, with trustworthy witnesses summoned for this. Immediately the notary shall require witnesses, of whom two or three are to be present at all acts, except at the final proclamation of the fathers. Likewise the promoter of the order shall say, in the hearing of all:

By the authority of the lord presidents it is commanded to all and each, both those already present here and those arriving at any hour, in virtue of holy obedience, that no one in any way reveal the secrets of this provincial chapter to any secular person, or to anyone not subject to our aforesaid chapter, to the detriment, disgrace, or burden of the order and its professed members. By the same authority likewise it is commanded to all and each that no one presume to speak elsewhere in the capitular places and proceedings to the lord presidents or to the officials of the chapter deputed and to be deputed, unless leave has been sought and obtained, and this while standing and with head uncovered, with humility, reverence, and subjection; or, if he wishes, let him present it in writing. Likewise, by the same authority it is enjoined on all and each who are bound to be present at this chapter that no one depart from the place of the chapter without leave, but remain until its end, under the penalty of contumacy and of those not coming to chapter.

Then the register of monasteries shall be read by the promoter or the notary, and the absentees shall be marked with a pen by one of them, as is customary. When these have been marked, the promoter shall accuse the contumacy of the absentees in these or similar words, saying:

Reverend fathers, lord presidents, I accuse the contumacy of the absent prelates who by law are bound to be present at this sacred provincial chapter, and I ask that a monition be decreed, to be executed at the doors of this monastery against the same contumacious men and against those rebellious toward the visitors, so that they may appear to show that they have obeyed the mandates of the chapter and have actually presented themselves to it; otherwise, to see themselves declared to have incurred the penalties of [unclear]. Let one of the presidents see to this.

We presidents, wishing to act more graciously and not to condemn anyone quickly, shall wait for the absentees until the following day, and, if necessary, longer, so that meanwhile the proxies of the absentees may also be examined: whether their absence ought deservedly to be excused, and whether the proctors themselves ought to be considered present. In addition, we decree a monition against the rebellious.

After this, if there is time, let them choose definitors from the abbots, who can give counsel and aid to the presidents in the business of the chapter. Likewise let them depute three or four from the same abbots to examine the proxies of the absentees after dinner, or at a fixed time, in an appointed place to which the proctors are to come, with this provision: that if any proxies are considered doubtful, they shall refer the examination to the lord presidents. The form of a sufficient proxy is expressly contained in the acts of the chapter.

Then the president may give advance warning to the visitors that, at a fixed time or hour which they shall determine, they be ready to present to the lord presidents the accounts and summaries of their visitations, according to the constitutions of the preceding fathers. And if the hour is late and nothing difficult now remains, they shall give leave to go to table, with one of the presidents saying in these or similar words:

Venerable fathers, since the hour has now become rather late and it is time for dinner, lest we delay you, weary as you are, any longer from refreshment, we now wish to put an end to these proceedings. Therefore let each man take his place at table according to the promoter’s ordering, with discipline; in silence and with thanksgiving let him eat what has been set before him.

The promoter of the order shall place the fathers in the refectory according to the date of each one’s prelacy, so far as can be done. And first the abbots shall sit, then the priors and provosts, thereafter the proctors of the absentees, and afterward the other simple brothers. This order of sitting, however, can rarely be arranged in this way because of the multitude of those sitting and

their unknown ages. And if the presidents wish to give any further admonition, let them do so, especially if there are any who differ from the others in their tonsure, so that after dinner they may see to it that they are properly shaved. Then the presidents shall conclude: “Our help is in the name of the Lord.” The others shall answer: “Who made heaven and earth.” And so let them go. But before they are dismissed let all be admonished that, at the first or second signal of the bell, all are again to be present in the chapter-place; and, if it seems good to the presidents, some penalty shall be imposed on those who arrive late.

After dinner. When the fathers have assembled together at the ringing, let them say the customary prayer, the president beginning it, which ought to be said on bended knees before every capitular act, as follows:

“Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love, who through diversity, etc. Alleluia, alleluia. Kyrie eleison. Kyrie eleison. Our Father.” One of the presidents, adding, shall say: “And lead us not into temptation.” The others shall respond: “But deliver us.” President: “Save your servants.” Response: “My God, who hope in you.” President: “Send them, O Lord, help from the holy place.” Response: “And from your Zion [unclear] them.” President: “Be to us, O Lord, a tower of strength.” Response: “From the face of the enemy.” President: “O Lord God of hosts, turn us.” Response: “And show us your face, and we shall be saved.” President: “O Lord, hear my prayer.” Response: “And let my cry come unto you.” President: “The Lord be with you. Let us pray.

“Stretch forth, O Lord, to your faithful the right hand of heavenly aid, so that they may seek you with all their heart, and may be worthy to obtain what they worthily ask. O Lord, by your inspiration go before our actions, and by your help carry them forward, so that every operation of ours may always begin from you, and, once begun, be ended through you. O God, who taught the hearts of the faithful by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, grant us in the same Spirit to know what is right, and always to rejoice in his consolation. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.”

These things shall be said by the president who gives the address, the others responding. After this the same president shall say, “Bless.” The others shall answer, “The Lord.” And he shall add: “If any one of you, reverend fathers, wishes to propose anything for the common good of the chapter, of the order, and of the persons of the same, let him set it forth confidently, with fear of the Lord, reverence, and humility; and we shall grant him a hearing with all patience.” But if anything necessary has been proposed, let the presidents, together with the definitors, have mature deliberation as to what is to be done in each matter. The presidents also sometimes customarily ask all the fathers in order, according to the requirement of the matters that arise: “If any fathers have complaints to propose against anyone, which could be remedied by us, let them propose them humbly and without disturbance, and in like manner we shall patiently hear them.” And he shall then add: “Likewise, if there are any brothers sent on behalf of their own people with testimonial letters to propose anything against anyone, let them present the letters and explain the reasons; we shall also hear them patiently and kindly.” After this, if there are any matters to be handled capitularly, let them be handled; and let one of the fathers be appointed who on the morrow shall sing Mass for the brothers. Then a brief exhortation can be given to the fathers, how they ought to conduct themselves in lodgings and in every place, in this or a similar manner:

“Venerable fathers, as you heard today when it was read from the Rule of Saint Benedict, according to which we are bound to live: the abbot who is set over the brothers ought to instruct them with holy doctrine and to go before them with examples of good works; and unless he presents both to his disciples, without doubt he will receive a fearful sentence in the strict examination of God’s judgment. For he is believed to act in Christ’s place in the monastery; therefore he must follow Christ. For he himself says: ‘He who ministers to me, let him follow me.’ As Christ fed his disciples by word and example, so also we who are his ministers, to our sheep

... by the teaching of holy instructions we may minister nourishment, and by the examples of good works we may offer incentives to virtue to the weaker. For the teaching of a pastor is useful to all; but examples of virtue are of greater benefit to the weak and untaught. Indeed, examples are more powerful than words, and it is better to teach by deed than by speech. We say these things for this reason: that, shining forth in good morals, we may furnish a good example in all things to those who see us. And, to come briefly to the point, we exhort your Paternities that in every place and time, and especially in lodgings, you do good, scandalizing no one; because the suspicion of the weak is so ready for the worse that by the scandal of one or a few the reputation of many is corrupted, which nevertheless, even with the praises of many, scarcely knows how to repair the infamy of a few. If nothing further remains, let the fathers be dismissed to their lodgings, [unclear] first that on the following day all come together for the Mass of the dead. And the notary, with the promoter of the order cooperating, shall write an admonition against the absentees in the form of a citation, to be affixed tomorrow, ex abundanti, to the doors of the monastery. Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth. And when these things have been said, let each go out to his lodging, except those who must remain. Monday.

Of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, with the prayers mentioned above. And the president shall say: Bless ye. They shall answer: The Lord. Then, if anything was begun yesterday, let it be continued. And the presidents shall instruct the notary to write the chapter proceedings. After this, at a suitable hour, the presidents shall withdraw to some more private place and hear the visitors one by one concerning the office enjoined upon them and performed by them, and concerning the conditions of the monasteries which they visited, both in spiritual and in temporal matters, and whether anywhere they were not admitted; and they shall produce copies of the letters which they left in the monasteries visited by them. But if any visitors are not present, they shall make such a report to the fathers either in writing or through their proctors. If any abbots have been notably accused in any matter by their visitors before the presidents, they shall be called, if it seems useful to the presidents, and admonished to amend themselves henceforth in the matters reported. Likewise, if the lord presidents cannot hear in person, let them appoint three or four fathers who shall hear and receive from the treasurers themselves an account in writing of what has been received and distributed; once reduced to writing, they shall send it to be deposited in the chest of the chapter. Then, when it is opportune, the promoter shall again accuse the contumacy of the absentees, and shall ask that they be condemned in expenses according to the constitutions of the order, under this form of words:

Reverend fathers, today, ex abundanti, I caused another citation to be affixed to the doors of the monastery against the abbots and other absentees who are bound to be present at this provincial chapter, so that they might still appear before your Paternities; otherwise they should know themselves bound to certain penalties. None of them has appeared or does appear. Therefore, lest they gain advantage from their disobedience, and that their punishment may serve as an example to the rest, I require you, reverend lord presidents, and ask that, according to the force and form of the constitutions of Benedict XII, you deign to proceed against the same absentees as contumacious, disobedient, and rebellious, according to the order of law, and to condemn them in expenses according to the named constitutions of the aforesaid Benedict.

Then one of the presidents, after the counsel of the others has been communicated for this purpose, shall proceed against the same persons in this way, sitting, under this form:

In the name of the Lord, by this our [unclear], which we, residing in the place of presidency, with the counsel and assent of those learned in law, pronounce, decree, and declare in these writings: that the lords N. and N., contumaciously absent, on account of their contumacy, in so great a sum of money, which by finding

they would have had to expend in staying at the chapter and in returning, if they had come; that they are to be condemned in double, according to the constitution of lord Pope Benedict XII. And we so condemn them in these writings, and declare that they are to be compelled to pay by ecclesiastical censures, and we compel the same persons. The assessment of these monies we have fixed at 2 Rhenish florins, to be paid without remission to our treasurers within [unclear] under penalty of excommunication, which, once that term has elapsed, they shall incur by these writings unless they have made satisfaction truly and effectively before the appointed day.

From these words the proper form for the process is to be taken. Or, if the lord presidents wish to act more mildly, then the last clause should be changed into this or a similar one: The assessment of these sums or quotas of money we reserve to ourselves or to our visitors. The presidents may, however, first cite them to hear the assessment made, which does not seem necessary, since the Benedictine constitution simply entrusts it to the lord presidents.

Then the promoter of the order should accuse the rebels and say: Reverend fathers, in the second place I accuse of contumacy a, b, c, abbots, who do not appear, neither by themselves nor by lawful proctors, although they have been sufficiently awaited, and who do not show that they have obeyed the concluded reform and have desisted from their contumacy and rebellion; and I ask that they be deemed contumacious, as they are, and that in their contumacy they be declared to have fallen under the sentence of excommunication contained in the processes of the past provincial chapters; and that appropriate letters be decreed thereupon, with further penalties, censures, and sentences, even to the invocation of the aid of the secular arm.

Then the same president should add: We deem the aforesaid absent persons contumacious, as they are. And he should add this sentence:

Having invoked the name of Christ, having God alone before our eyes, by this our sentence which, while residing in this place of presidency, we deliver in these writings with the counsel and assent of those learned in the law, we pronounce, decree, and declare: that the lords a, b, c, abbots, and a, b, c, conventuals, contumaciously absent, because of their contumacy and open rebellion, in that they damnably refused in the chapters to receive and effectively enter into the concluded holy and due regular observance, and, not desisting from this rebellion of theirs, did not appear, nor did they take care to allege lawful or reasonable causes why they should by no means be bound to this, have fallen under the sentence of excommunication according to the tenor of our processes in the past chapters, or in the last chapter celebrated at N.; and that they as such are publicly to be denounced and are denounced. And we command that our necessary letters be issued thereupon, also under other censures and sentences, decreeing by these presents even inclusively to the invocation of the aid of the secular arm.

It should be noted that the lord presidents, against absent contumacious persons, may also, if it pleases them, proceed otherwise: namely, that in the recess they set down that within a certain time they are to come to terms with them, or with the visitors, or with others to whom they have given authority, a term being given as canonical warning. But if they neglect this, once the appointed term has elapsed, they are excommunicated by the fact itself, to be absolved by no one except by the presidents themselves or by the visitors. But if it has been done thus, then they should take care to bring a process of this kind to their certain notice.

After the sentence has been passed, the absent persons should be cited again to hear and see the expenses assessed on the morrow, under this or a similar form, and let it be affixed in the evening:

By mandate of the reverend and venerable fathers, the lords presidents of the black monks of the Order of Saint Benedict of the province of Mainz and the diocese of Bamberg, all and singular abbots, provosts, priors, and the others who ought to be concerned, and who think themselves concerned, of the province and diocese of the same, are cited to appear on Wednesday after the Sunday on which Jubilate is sung, at the sixth hour in the morning, by themselves or their lawful proctors, in the monastery N., before the aforesaid

by the said presidents, to see and hear a taxation made of all and each of the expenses in which, by the aforesaid lord presidents, according to the constitution of lord Pope Benedict XII, because of their manifold contumacy and for other causes to be expressed in the term, they are judicially [condemned?]; and the other things appropriate concerning the premises are to be declared and pronounced; and the [unclear] and necessary proceedings thereupon are to be decreed and granted, with the customary intimation. And whether they appear or not, nevertheless, through those same presidents, in the premises, as the order of reason shall dictate, it will undoubtedly proceed, the absence of those cited notwithstanding. In testimony of these things the seals of two presidents have been affixed to the presents. Given in the year of the Lord [unclear]. Let the [unclear] subscribe themselves. This citation, as has been said above, is to be affixed under vespers or compline to the doors of the monastery or church.

After dinner on Monday.

If the matters written above can be dispatched before dinner, well. If not, let them complete them in the vacant time, as shall seem opportune to all the presidents. Likewise let the legate and the last chapter of the recess be read; and if any commissions have been made to anyone, let their executions be examined. Then, if nothing remains, let the fathers be dismissed to their lodgings, to return tomorrow at the sixth hour at the ringing of the bell.

The Third Day.

On the third day in the morning let the bell be rung, and let the Mass of the Blessed Virgin Mary be sung solemnly by one of the fathers appointed to it on the preceding evening, at which all the others shall be present. When it is finished, let them go to the chapter, and let the customary prayer be made, Veni sancte spiritus, etc. And let one of the presidents say, Benedicite. And when the response is made, Dominus, let him continue if anything was omitted yesterday. Likewise afterward let attention be turned to the order; and if anything new is to be established, let it be inserted this day in the recess. Likewise, if any replies are to be given or written to princes or to others, let them be made and dispatched by the counsel of the fathers. If the treasurers are not present, let some be appointed who shall collect the expenses, namely three Rhenish florins from each abbot, this day, recording what has been collected on a schedule, lest perhaps anyone, which God forbid, pretend that he has given what he has not given. Likewise let some be deputed as assistance to the notary, who know how to arrange the recess, so that by evening after dinner it may be completed. Likewise, if the necessity of the order requires it, let a proportional contribution be imposed on all the monasteries, and let the cause and form be inserted in the recess, which all shall be bound to pay under penalties to be expressed in the same, according to the constitutions of Pope Benedict XII. And it is to be noted that the lord presidents, with the definitors, can impose a contribution on others according to the Benedictine constitution without their consent; yet they themselves are not free from this sort of contribution. For what they impose on others, they themselves ought first to bear. That it is theirs to impose a contribution is sufficiently shown in the same constitutions, in these words in chapter five:

“We establish and ordain that in the same chapters, notwithstanding any contradiction or absence whatsoever, for liberties, necessities, utilities, common expenses, and other customary things, since a burden divided into parts is borne more lightly, collections, subsidies, or contributions are to be made, imposed, and proclaimed by apostolic authority, according to the judgment of the presidents or definitors, as regards a provincial chapter of this kind.” Meanwhile also, if it shall seem good to the lord presidents, let the common expenses of the chapter be assessed with the father of the house, as is usually done.

After dinner.

When dinner has been completed, at the signal of the bell let them at once assemble as above; and when the president has said Benedicite, and the response Dominus has been made, let the chapter be continued. Then, at the command of the presidents, let the recess be read, which should already be completed. At its end there should be contained the place and day of the future chapter, and the other things which customarily ought to be done. And it is to be noted that no more than two years ought to elapse between the chapter celebrated and the chapter to be celebrated, according to the constitution of Benedict

..., whose words on this matter are these. But what is permitted concerning the provincial chapter to be celebrated from three years to three years, in order to remove the scruple of any hesitation, we wish to be referred to a sound understanding: namely, that when the provincial chapter has been celebrated in one year, it may be omitted in the next following year, and be held in every third year following. Yet this must be noted: that the lord presidents, if there is need, can anticipate the term, and likewise prolong it.

When everything has been completed, after the notary and witnesses have gone out, let the fathers proclaim themselves before the presidents, six or seven [unclear], beginning with the juniors and continuing to the presidents themselves inclusive, and let them receive the salutary penances imposed on them. Then let them all read in like manner, except one president: “I confess to God, to blessed Mary, to all the saints, and to you, father, that I have sinned exceedingly, through my fault, by pride, thought, speech, deed, and omission; I beseech you, pray for me.” And then that president should read the absolution as follows:

“May almighty God, through the intercession of blessed Mary and of all the saints, have mercy on you, and forgive you all your sins, and lead you to eternal life. Amen.

“By the authority of almighty God and of the ecclesiastical keys granted in this respect to our order, we restore you from the censures of the Church and to participation in the sacraments, and we dispense with you and rehabilitate you for the execution of the things to be done, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.”

And when some psalm has been imposed for satisfaction, let all rise, and the same president, kneeling before the other presidents, should read “I confess to God.” One of the presidents should read over him the absolution as above, with the psalm.

And note that this absolution is one of jurisdiction; nor should there be placed in it that clause which many thought ought to be added: “and from your sins.” For the sacramental absolution, which a particular confession of sins ought to precede, has this clause. Likewise it should be known that this absolution avails only, namely absolving from censures if anyone had incurred them by neglecting the statutes of the order and of the chapter. And as sacramental absolution absolves from guilt, so that of jurisdiction absolves from temporal and spiritual penalty. When these things have been done, let an end be imposed on each matter. Yet it should be known that if some utility or necessity is imminent, the said lord presidents can prolong the chapter further, until everything is determined well and maturely. At the end, one of the presidents, if time permits, should deliver to the fathers a brief exhortation before the blessing, on these or similar matters:

“Venerable fathers, since now, with God’s favor, we have celebrated this provincial chapter of ours, lest, as we depart from one another, we forget because of the multitude of them the things that we have heard, listen patiently to the brief admonition that I make. We exhort you first, that each of you remember continually what the Rule says: ‘Let the abbot know that the fault of the shepherd falls upon him, whatever less of usefulness the father of the household shall have been able to find in his sheep,’ etc.”

And he should add by way of exhortation, as the Lord shall grant, concerning keeping pure religion, concerning faithfully carrying out profession, concerning peace and charity and goodwill toward all, etc. Finally, that they depart from their lodgings with due honesty, after debts have been paid, with the knowledge of their host, not secretly but openly, etc. And that the abbots publish the statutes of this chapter to each of their subjects, and cause two conventual masses to be sung, one for the living, another for the deceased brethren of our order, and other prayers imposed to be fulfilled; and that the recess be read publicly in their monasteries to the brethren in necessary matters.

When these things have been completed, let the blessing be given by the president, as is customary, with all bowing moderately:

“Save your servants, my God, who hope in you.

“The Lord be with you.

“And with your spirit.

“Be present, Lord, to our supplications, and dispose the way of your servants in the prosperity of your salvation, so that among all [unclear].”

the ways and changes of this life may always be protected by your aid; through Christ our Lord. When these things have been completed, let each go to his own affairs, except the presidents and officials, if any have matters to arrange, compute, or settle. I have written these things only concerning the manner and order of celebrating a provincial chapter; although not everything to be done is contained in it, nevertheless many things are included here that are useful for such matters. Each item also does not refuse to undergo the examination of the lord presidents.

Bull of the Council of Basel concerning the reform of the Order of Saint Benedict throughout the province of Mainz.

The most holy general synod of Basel, lawfully assembled in the Holy Spirit, representing the universal Church: to the beloved sons of the Church, all and singular presidents and visitors appointed anywhere, and to be appointed in future, for future provincial chapters of the black monks, greeting and the blessing of almighty God.

Among the manifold cares by which we are distracted by the varieties of affairs and business arising in the universal Church, that one especially stirs and moves our minds by which regular orders and places devoted to the yoke of holiness may flourish again in spiritual things; whence we willingly expend effective solicitude for this, that those orders and places themselves which have incurred the reproach of deformity may be led back to the paths of due reform, and, with the Lord continually directing them, may receive increase in those same spiritual things and also in temporal things.

Indeed, a petition lately presented to us by the beloved sons of the Church, religious men of the order of the black monks of the [unclear] nation, contained that, although some time ago the fathers had included salutary articles concerning the reform of that order, nevertheless some of the subjects of this order and nation, when provincial visitors or reformers come to them according to the form of those articles, do not permit themselves to be reformed, <[unclear: about one line damaged]>

XXXV

taking occasion from the fact that such articles did not proceed from us, and that, if we should ordain any reform, they would receive it.

Wherefore, on behalf of the religious men of this nation it was humbly supplicated to us that we would deign to command that reform be made in all monasteries in which the greater regular observance does not flourish, of the nation and order, according to the content and form of the aforesaid articles.

We therefore, whose principal concern this is, and who have been gathered into one by divine providence for this purpose, that the salutary reform of the Church of God, in head and in members, may be steadily made and may persevere, considering that articles of this kind are conformable to written law and to the Rule of blessed Benedict, and that they ought to have place and to be observed not only in the aforesaid nation but in all and singular other nations, monasteries, and places of the said order, as regards such reform, and wishing also to provide opportunely concerning the premises, by these writings command your discretion that you and each one of you, as it pertains to the office of each and shall pertain according to the time, whenever it shall seem expedient to your consciences, which we burden as to this matter, should faithfully and diligently exercise the office of visitation and reform in all monasteries and places of the often-said order in which the greater regular observance does not flourish, according to the content and form of the said articles, the texts of which we have caused to be entered below word for word, by the authority of the universal Church.

For we, so that the desired fruits may follow from the zeal of visitation and reform of this kind, [authorize you concerning] all and singular abbots and other presidents of the monasteries and places which it shall fall to you to visit, and persons of whatever status, rank, order, and condition they may exist, according to the quality and demand of the offenses perpetrated by them from time to time, and the canonical sanctions and regular statutes of the said order, as you shall perceive to be fitting for the salvation of souls and for the condition and immunities of those monasteries and places

of correcting, and of striking with due penalties; likewise of absolving the abbots and other presidents and persons of this sort, and each of them, if they shall seek this by these letters, from all and singular sentences, censures, and penalties of excommunication, suspension, and interdict by which they shall for the time be found bound, or which perhaps may happen to be promulgated against them in any way through the execution of this office, in the customary form of the Church, after a salutary penance has been enjoined upon them according to the measure of their fault, together with the other things that by law are to be enjoined. Likewise, of publishing and intimating the aforesaid articles, and of causing them to be received and observed by all subjects; and of disposing, ordering, establishing, and executing all and singular things necessary or opportune in the premises and concerning them in any way; and of restraining contradictors and rebels by ecclesiastical censure and other remedies of law, invoking for this, if need be, the aid of the secular arm. By the authority of the universal Church, by the tenor of the presents, we grant to you and to each of you full and free faculty: notwithstanding apostolic constitutions, statutes, and customs of the aforesaid monasteries, places, and order, strengthened by oath, apostolic confirmation, or any other firmness whatsoever, and all other things whatsoever to the contrary. Or if it has been granted by the Apostolic See to the monasteries, places, and order, to the abbots and other presidents and persons, or to any persons whatsoever, jointly or severally, that they are in no way bound to admit anyone to visitation or otherwise beyond and contrary to the privileges or indults granted to them, and that they cannot be compelled to this, or excommunicated, or that they themselves or the monasteries and places of this sort cannot be placed under interdict or suspended, by letters not making full and express mention, word for word, of such an indult; and notwithstanding any apostolic privileges, exemptions, and indulgences, general or special, of whatever tenor they may be, by which the execution of your jurisdiction in this matter, not expressed or not wholly inserted in the presents, could in any way be hindered, which, as regards this, we do not wish to avail them in any way.

Concerning Absolution.

We wish, moreover, that each of the same presidents and persons whom you shall think fit to absolve from sentences, censures, and penalties of this sort, or from any one of them, must and shall be bound to render, to each person to whom satisfaction may perhaps have to be made on that account, that satisfaction within a competent peremptory term to be fixed by you, once any canonical impediment has ceased. Otherwise, when that term has passed, they shall fall back by that very fact into the former sentences, censures, and penalties. The tenor of the aforesaid articles, as they have preceded, follows and is as follows.

Articles for Reformation.

Because regular discipline and the holiness of religion have almost wholly fallen, and have miserably collapsed, to the grave scandal of the whole order of Black Monks, and to the dishonor, reproach, and [contempt?] of all professed members of the same order, and, what is more dreadful, to the deadly harm of the salvation of souls. For alas, every adornment of religion has been taken away from it; and that which lately could glory in the Lord, saying, “I am black” in the lowliness of habit, “and beautiful” in holiness of morals and of conduct, now alas, the once holy monastic simplicity has been perverted into wantonness and insolence, so that no image of former holiness now seems to survive either in fact or even in appearance.

Therefore we, the abbots and the other religious of the said order, gathered in the sacred Council of Basel, wishing with highest desires and with one zeal to provide against such and so enormous scandals, have come and been gathered into one for the reformation of the same order, lest henceforth it suffer a more grievous ruin, which God forbid; devoutly and wholesomely applying ourselves with daily labors to the aforesaid reformation, we have set forth certain beginnings and foundations of religion, so that, by beginning from these, the deformed monasteries may be able to advance toward the fruit of monastic profession; and, by way of abundant caution, from the rule

[unclear] of the most blessed Benedict our father and from the constitutions of the lord Pope Benedict XII of happy memory, which we judged ought to be observed in all the monasteries and places of the said order in which the stricter regular observance does not flourish.

Yet on this account we do not intend, just as we cannot, to derogate in any way from the other things contained in the aforesaid Rule, even if they are not now explained by us, or from the praiseworthy constitutions of the fathers and the stricter observances, so as to lessen the obligation by which the religious of the said order are bound to them as before.

First, On the Divine Office. Article 1.

Since the said Rule of Saint Benedict took very solicitous care concerning the divine service, we, following it, ordain that the divine office, both by day and by night, be celebrated devoutly, deliberately, with pauses, not hurried through, not cut short, at the proper hours, as is contained in the Rule of our most blessed father. And that, as soon as the signal has been heard, leaving everything that they have in their hands, they shall hasten there with the greatest speed, yet with gravity, lest frivolity find fuel; so that nothing be placed before the work of God.

And lest they be able to excuse themselves on the pretext of ignorance, saying that the signal was not heard, we will that the ringing for Matins, which is to begin at midnight or thereabouts, and for Prime and Vespers, continue for at least more than a quarter of an hour.

But anyone who does not come to the aforesaid office shall be punished without remission, as is contained in the Rule.

On Confession and the Celebration of Masses. Article 2.

We also will and ordain that the abbots and the others of the aforesaid order confess, celebrate, and receive communion, as is contained in the constitutions of Pope Benedict XII concerning the celebration of Masses.

And that all those who, according to the sanctions of law and of Benedict, ought to be established in sacred orders or in the order of priesthood, shall within a year be promoted to them; and against those who are negligent the visitors shall proceed as they can by law.

On the Daily Chapter of Faults. Article 3.

We further will and ordain that every day, in places where there are six monks, and in other places where it is customary, after Prime if only one Mass is said, but if two are said, after the first-mentioned Mass or at another customary hour, the daily chapter shall be held, in which, after the martyrology and the reading of the Rule, which shall be explained in the vernacular by the one presiding over that chapter, or by another whom he has ordered, before proceeding to other matters, the faults and excesses of the negligent or delinquent shall be punished.

On the Books and Ornaments of the Church. Article 4.

We will that each abbot or president, when he has come to his monastery, immediately provide within a month for clean and good vessels and a place where the holy Eucharist may be kept; and also that the books, with the other ornaments concerning the divine office and the monastery, be kept under diligent custody.

On the Form and Decency of Clothing and Tonsure. Article 5.

Since, through the propriety of outward habit, the professed and novices of the said order ought to show decency of morals and of religion, we decree and ordain that all wear large and broad tonsures, so that the circle of them does not exceed the space or width of two transverse fingers. And that they conduct themselves decently in clothes, habits, and footwear, according to Clementine Ne in agro and the constitution of the aforesaid Pope Benedict XII on the form and decency of garments: namely, that they wear tunics and garments next beneath the upper habit, of black or brown color according to the custom usually observed among them, round and reaching to the ankles, not split, nor marked by any other deformity, having broad sleeves extended as far as the fists, in no way buttoned or tied; yet not so broad that their width may extend beyond the fist with the thumb raised, nor, around the mouth of the elbow, as the abuse of some has it, be stretched farther;

…so that the arm may easily be turned and drawn in. Let them be content with almuces of skins in place of hoods. Yet in respectable places, in which they have been accustomed to wear them, they may, with the abbot's permission, use honest hoods, slit over the shoulders to a length of at least four transverse fingers. In their garments let them not wear silk-stuff for linings, nor minever or other costly furs; but let them use the skins of young lambs or lambkins for the said linings, or at least other non-costly cloths. Nor let the linings appear above the collar, or on the hems of garments or of sleeves, in any way.

Of the habit of those who travel. Article 6. Moreover, when it befalls them to set out beyond the monastery, let them wear the floccus or the cowl or the cappa; and beneath the cappa, if they have worn it, let them have a cowl or a scapular.

Of the habit of novices and lay brothers. Article 7. Let novices use the cowl, open inside the monastery and outside on either side. But let the lay brothers use the scapular with a hood attached to it, closed, inside and outside the monastery.

Of the length and width of the garments. Article 8. Since some use the aforesaid habits more ample and long, and others less than they ought, on account of the length and width of the aforesaid [garments] we have determined that the following be inserted in the present [statutes], which we wish to be commonly observed. And first, beginning with the hood of the floccus: we ordain that its width not reach the elbow-bone, by the thickness of two transverse fingers, nor be allowed to be tighter, or so short, but that it extend to the middle of the elbow and the upper bone near the shoulder; and behind let it extend at least as far as the belt, nor beyond it by four fingers. And let the length of the sleeves extend by one cubit beyond the hand and no more; and let their width not exceed another cubit and a half. Yet let the floccus below be made so wide that the step may easily be made

through it. And what has been said of the floccus we wish to be understood of the cowl with sleeves, when they have none set apart. But within the monastery, in places where there have been twelve monks, let all use the floccus or large cowls. In other places, where there has not been so great a congregation, let them use cowls, not flocci—except the president of the monastery and the second after him, whom we wish to wear the floccus in every case. Yet in [divine] works and in the divine office let them be able to wear, beneath the alb, and when riding, beneath the cappa, a scapular of a width of at least half a cubit. And let them wear high boots or boots or strapped shoes, such that their width comprehends a space of four fingers, [reaching] from the shin over the ankle. For if in any of the aforesaid matters they shall not have worn the habits (as is set forth above), then, beyond the penalties inflicted by law, we wish them to be so punished—by their superiors in their religious house, or by the superior if they have none, [or] by the visitors of the provincial chapter—that it may serve as an example to the rest.

That the monks live in common in the refectory without the eating of meat. Article 9. Item, that the brothers live and eat in common in the refectory, in which let no one at all eat meat. And let the visitors be diligent to cause the constitution of Benedict concerning the eating of and abstinence from meats to be observed inviolably.

Of the table-reading of the brothers. Article 10. Let the sacred reading not be lacking; and let him who is to read for the whole week enter upon it on Sunday after the blessing, as [is laid down] in the Rule, chapter 38, concerning the weekly reader.

How the monks are to sleep. Article 11. Let the monks sleep individually, clothed, in individual beds in the same place if it can be done, or at least in tens or twenties; but not in [separate] chambers, especially if these have not been suitably partitioned—so that the bedding in them may be seen aptly and clearly, according to the manner of their way of life

according to the disposition of the abbot; and let them not use feather mattresses.

If, however, chambers are found in the dormitory, we command that they be destroyed by the visitors or by their mandate, or suitably barred off.

On silence in four places. Article 12. Silence is to be observed in the oratory, the dormitory, the refectory, and the cloister. And after Compline let no one be permitted to say anything, except as is contained in the Rule. And before the said Compline let the Conference of the Fathers be read, or something else edifying.

On the porter of the monastery. Article 13. At the gate of each monastery let one prudent and discreet porter or doorkeeper be appointed, so that without the permission of the abbot or of another presiding officer no freedom of leaving it may be granted to anyone. For if anyone shall go out without permission of this kind, let him be subjected to fitting and due penalties, as is provided in the constitutions of Benedict XII concerning the permission ordained for going outside the monastery. Let him also be attentive that he in no way permit women to enter the monastery.

That no one from the order of mendicants be received into our order. Article 14.
